root.note: Wiktionary derives Late Latin pasta from Greek pastá, ‘barley porridge’, itself from pastós ‘sprinkled’. The route is generally accepted, but the Greek step rests on a few late sources.

history: Pasta is first of all ‘dough’, and only then ‘the thing you boil’. Late Latin had pasta for a paste or dough, and most dictionaries trace it to Greek pastá, a porridge of barley sprinkled with salt or broth. In Italian the word covers a lot: la pasta is the dough, pasta fresca and pasta secca are two kinds of noodles, and le paste are small pastries you buy at a bar or pasticceria. When you want the dish, you can say pastasciutta, ‘dry pasta’, as opposed to pasta in brodo, pasta in soup. English borrowed pasta from Italian only in the 1830s. It already had paste and pastry from the same ancestor, through French.
historyEinfach: Pasta first meant ‘dough’. Late Latin used pasta for a soft mixture. Italians use the word for the dough, for the dish and for small sweet cakes (le paste). English has the words paste and pastry from the same old word. English took pasta from Italian in the 1830s.

elsewhere.text: English borrowed the dish name directly from Italian. Paste and pastry arrived much earlier through Old French.
